params.text:
Rescue breaths (30:2)

If you are trained and willing, combine compressions with rescue breaths in a ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths. After 30 compressions, open the airway again with head-tilt chin-lift, pinch the nose, seal your lips around their mouth and blow steadily until the chest just begins to rise. Give two breaths, then return to compressions.

Compression-only CPR: if you are untrained, unwilling, or unable to give rescue breaths, do continuous chest compressions without stopping. This is far better than doing nothing.

Using an AED

An automated external defibrillator (AED) analyses the heart rhythm and, if it is needed, delivers a controlled electric shock to help the heart re-establish a normal beat. It is designed for untrained members of the public, so you cannot easily go wrong: turn it on as soon as it arrives and do exactly what the spoken voice prompts tell you.

  • Attach the pads to the person's bare, dry chest exactly as shown in the pictures on the pads — one below the right collarbone, the other on the left side below the armpit. If a second rescuer is there, keep chest compressions going while the pads are put on.
  • Stand clear to analyse: make sure nobody touches the person while the AED analyses the heart rhythm.
  • Shock safely: if a shock is advised, make sure everyone is clear, then press the shock button. Do not touch the person during analysis or shock.
  • Restart compressions: immediately restart compressions after the shock and keep following the AED's prompts.

Staying safe and special situations

The AED will tell everyone to stand clear while it analyses the rhythm and while it shocks; nobody must be touching the casualty at that moment.

  • Dry the chest: wipe off sweat or water so the pads stick and the shock is not spread across wet skin.
  • Move hazards: keep pads clear of jewellery, medication patches and any implanted pacemaker lump.
  • Oxygen away: move any oxygen mask away from the chest before a shock is given.
  • Children: for a child use paediatric pads or a paediatric setting if available, but never delay using a standard AED if that is all you have.

Follow the voice prompts and get back to compressions the instant you are told to.

params.question: An AED has arrived and is analysing the heart rhythm. What should everyone do?

answers.text: Keep doing chest compressions to be safe

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Movement interferes with the AED's analysis. Everyone must stand clear while it analyses.

answers.text: Make sure nobody is touching the person while it analyses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Touching the person can disrupt the analysis, and you must also be clear before any shock is delivered.

answers.text: Turn the AED off and restart it

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Leave the AED on and simply follow its voice prompts.

answers.text: Remove the pads and reposition them elsewhere

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No. Leave the pads in the positions shown and let the AED analyse and advise.

params.textField: An AED will only deliver a *shock* if the heart rhythm actually needs one. Attach the *pads* to the casualty’s bare, dry chest exactly as shown in the pictures. Then simply follow the spoken *prompts* the machine gives you. Before any shock, make sure that nobody is *touching* the casualty. Keep giving good chest compressions and only *pause* them when the AED tells you to.
